question: What fraction of MAS-AIRM expectations can be automatically checked from artefacts, semi-automated with human attestation, or only documented?
method: Each of the 51 expectation paragraphs takes the best automatability class among the controls implementing it; paragraphs with no implementing control count as doc. Classes and their justifications are in src/airm/controls/controls.yaml.

1.6.heading: Introduction
1.6.justification: A framework-adequacy judgement for the board, not an artefact property.

1.7.heading: Introduction
1.7.justification: A review cadence is evidenceable but whether the review genuinely addressed new risks is a judgement.

2.2.heading: Application of the Guidelines
2.2.justification: No control in this catalogue implements the paragraph, so this toolkit offers no way to check it.

2.5.heading: Application of the Guidelines
2.5.justification: Policy existence and content are organisational facts. The toolkit can hold the policy pointer and flag the §2.5(f) review as overdue, nothing more.

3.2.heading: AI Oversight
3.2.justification: A framework-adequacy judgement for the board, not an artefact property.

3.3.heading: AI Oversight
3.3.justification: MAS removed the prescriptive dedicated-committee requirement (Response to Feedback §5.3), so what remains is an outcome the FI must demonstrate, not a structure a tool can detect.

3.4.heading: AI Oversight
3.4.justification: The toolkit can see whether a confirmation exists but cannot evaluate an FI's appetite statement, which §3.4(b) leaves to the board.

3.5.heading: AI Oversight
3.5.justification: An incident log is machine-readable and the toolkit maintains one; whether escalation happened in time is a process judgement.

3.6.heading: AI Oversight
3.6.justification: An accountability narrative, evidenced by minutes and reporting, not by data.

4.1.heading: Key AI Risk Management Systems, Policies and Procedures
4.1.justification: Whether a control function is designated for each of the three processes is decidable from the register's own metadata.

4.2.heading: AI Identification
4.2.justification: Whether an embedded component from a material provider carries an independent assessment is decidable from the register's own fields.

4.3.heading: AI Identification
4.3.justification: Whether a control function is designated for each of the three processes is decidable from the register's own metadata.

4.4.heading: AI Identification
4.4.justification: The existence of a shadow-AI policy and of technical controls is evidenceable; the adequacy of coverage is not, and no accepted metric for shadow-AI coverage exists (see the gap table).

4.5.heading: AI Inventory
4.5.justification: A last-reviewed date is machine-readable, but whether the frequency is appropriate is an FI judgement that MAS deliberately leaves open (Response to Feedback §6.18).

4.6.heading: AI Inventory
4.6.justification: A declared mapping in the register; presence is decidable.

4.7.heading: AI Inventory
4.7.justification: Each attribute is a field of the register; presence is decidable without judgement. Adequacy of the content is not checked, which is why the control is about capture, not quality.

4.8.heading: AI Inventory
4.8.justification: Footnote 25 names four attributes; each maps to a field of the agent extension.

4.9.heading: AI Inventory
4.9.justification: Whether a control function is designated for each of the three processes is decidable from the register's own metadata.

4.10.heading: AI Risk Materiality Assessment
4.10.justification: The rubric is deterministic, so the rating and its agreement with the recorded rating are both decidable. The rubric itself is the toolkit's proposal, not a MAS method.

4.11.heading: AI Risk Materiality Assessment
4.11.justification: The rubric is deterministic, so the rating and its agreement with the recorded rating are both decidable. The rubric itself is the toolkit's proposal, not a MAS method.

4.12.heading: AI Risk Materiality Assessment
4.12.justification: The rubric is deterministic, so the rating and its agreement with the recorded rating are both decidable. The rubric itself is the toolkit's proposal, not a MAS method.

4.13.heading: AI Risk Materiality Assessment
4.13.justification: Whether a control function is designated for each of the three processes is decidable from the register's own metadata.

5.1.heading: AI Life Cycle Controls
5.1.justification: Presence of an owner and developer party is decidable from the register.

5.2.heading: AI Life Cycle Controls
5.2.justification: Whether a pilot records a scope-limiting guardrail (rate limit, allowlist, step cap or human checkpoint) is decidable from the register.

5.3.heading: AI Life Cycle Controls
5.3.justification: A recorded plan is checkable; whether it was tested and is operationally feasible under a range of conditions is not, and no evidence convention exists (see the gap table).

5.4.heading: Data Management
5.4.justification: The register records a classification; whether it is correct is a data-governance judgement.

5.5.heading: Transparency and Explainability
5.5.justification: "Appropriate level" is the judgement MAS explicitly keeps contextual (Response to Feedback §10.12-§10.15); only the existence of disclosures and explanation methods is evidenceable.

5.6.heading: Transparency and Explainability
5.6.justification: The existence of a disclosure artefact and a redress channel is checkable; adequacy for the audience is a judgement.

5.7.heading: Fairness
5.7.justification: A fairness report with metric values is machine-readable and can be threshold-checked, but there is no universally applicable metric (Response to Feedback §10.21), so metric choice and threshold are FI judgements requiring attestation.

5.8.heading: Fairness
5.8.justification: A fairness report with metric values is machine-readable and can be threshold-checked, but there is no universally applicable metric (Response to Feedback §10.21), so metric choice and threshold are FI judgements requiring attestation.

5.9.heading: Human Oversight
5.9.justification: Whether an oversight arrangement is recorded at all is decidable; this control checks presence, and the adequacy judgement sits in AIRM-5.9-OVERSIGHT-EFFECTIVENESS.

5.10.heading: Third-Party AI Management
5.10.justification: An eval result scoped to the use case is machine-readable; whether it compensates adequately for vendor opacity is a judgement (Response to Feedback §9.10).

5.11.heading: Third-Party AI Management
5.11.justification: Whether an independent assessment is recorded for each component is decidable from the register. Whether the assessment covers the right risks is not, so the evidence list asks for the assessment scope.

5.12.heading: Selection
5.12.justification: A selection note is checkable for existence; the balance it strikes is a judgement, and MAS softened this from a requirement to justify in all cases (Response to Feedback §10.24).

5.13.heading: Selection
5.13.justification: A selection note is checkable for existence; the balance it strikes is a judgement, and MAS softened this from a requirement to justify in all cases (Response to Feedback §10.24).

5.14.heading: Evaluation and Testing
5.14.justification: Thresholds and measured values are machine-comparable once recorded, so a breach is detectable; whether the measures and thresholds are the right ones is an FI judgement that MAS declines to prescribe (Response to Feedback §10.28-§10.29).

5.15.heading: Evaluation and Testing
5.15.justification: Whether a pilot records a scope-limiting guardrail (rate limit, allowlist, step cap or human checkpoint) is decidable from the register.

5.16.heading: Technology and Cybersecurity Risks
5.16.justification: Declared approved tools and permissions are register fields; their presence is decidable and is the precondition for the observed-versus-approved audit in `airm.evals`.

5.17.heading: Reproducibility and Auditability
5.17.justification: Whether documentation is linked at all is decidable from the register. Whether it would let someone replicate the evaluation is the judgement left to the reviewer, which is why the evidence list asks for the reproducibility statement.

5.18.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.18.justification: Whether a review status other than "not reviewed" is on record is decidable; the depth of the review is the reviewer's judgement.

5.19.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.19.justification: Independence of the named validator from owner, developer, deployer and operator is decidable from role records; whether the challenge was effective is not.

5.20.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.20.justification: Whether a review status other than "not reviewed" is on record is decidable; the depth of the review is the reviewer's judgement.

5.21.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.21.justification: A governance workflow fact, outside the toolkit's view.

5.22.heading: Pre-Deployment Reviews
5.22.justification: Presence and date of a penetration test, red-team report and go-live checklist are checkable; their depth is a judgement, and MAS prescribes no methodology (Response §10.39).

5.23.heading: Post-Deployment Monitoring and Review
5.23.justification: Whether trace logging is enabled is a register field, and the toolkit can additionally audit an actual trace against approved tool scope.

5.24.heading: Post-Deployment Monitoring and Review
5.24.justification: A due date and a last-validated date are comparable, so an overdue re-validation is detectable; the appropriate interval is an FI judgement.

5.25.heading: Change Management
5.25.justification: Presence of a change-notification term is a register field.

5.26.heading: Change Management
5.26.justification: For a retired use case the presence of a decommissioning record is decidable; adequacy of secure removal is not, and is covered by the data security control.

6.1.heading: AI Risk Management Capabilities
6.1.justification: Training completion records exist but competence is not inspectable from artefacts; MAS also allows role-based training checks instead of individual assessment (Response §11.9).

6.2.heading: AI Risk Management Capabilities
6.2.justification: Training completion records exist but competence is not inspectable from artefacts; MAS also allows role-based training checks instead of individual assessment (Response §11.9).

6.3.heading: Technology Infrastructure for AI
6.3.justification: A capacity and resilience judgement made outside this toolkit.

verdicts.hypothesis: H1(a) auto share is below 50% of expectation paragraphs
H1(a) semi is the largest class
H1(b) Section 4 auto share exceeds Section 3

threats_to_validity: The classification is the authors' judgement, not MAS'. Each row carries a written justification so it can be disputed individually.
A clause is auto *relative to this implementation*: it depends on what the toolkit ingests. A richer integration would move some semi clauses to auto.
Single annotator, so no inter-rater agreement is available. The full table is published for challenge.
Taking the best class per paragraph flatters automatability: a paragraph with one auto and four doc controls counts as auto.
